title: Perfil del Bioma: Selva Tropical Húmeda (Amazonía)
text: Tropical rainforests receive >2,000 mm/year precipitation and maintain high year-round temperatures (25-28°C). The Amazon loses ~600 km² annually to deforestation. NDVI shows seasonal patterns peaking in dry season (Aug-Nov) when reduced cloud cover increases photosynthesis.

title: Perfil del Bioma: Alta Montaña y Glaciares Tropicales (Andes)
text: Tropical glaciers in the Andes (Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador) are rapidly retreating. Average temperature at 5,000m has increased ~1°C since 1980. The Peruvian Cordillera Blanca has lost ~48% of its ice mass since 1970. Glacial meltwater supports ~3M people downstream.

title: Perfil del Bioma: Desierto Costero Peruano (Sechura)
text: The Peruvian coastal desert receives <25 mm/year rainfall. The Humboldt Current keeps temperatures 5-10°C below the tropical average. El Niño events bring heavy rainfall (up to 500mm in weeks) and transform the landscape temporarily.

title: Perfil del Bioma: Hielo Marino Ártico (Svalbard)
text: Arctic sea ice has declined ~13% per decade since 1978. The Svalbard region (78°N) shows faster than average decline: summer ice cover down ~40% since 2000. This amplifies warming through albedo feedback—less ice means more solar absorption.

title: Control de Falsos Descubrimientos con Benjamini-Hochberg en Mapas de Tendencia
text: Cuando se testean miles de puntos (celdas) simultáneamente, muchos aparecerán 'significativos' por azar. El método de Benjamini-Hochberg controla la tasa de falsos descubrimientos (FDR): si q=0.10, solo el ~10% de las celdas marcadas como significativas serán falsos positivos.

title: Climate Change: How the Earth is Changing
text: Earth's average surface temperature has risen about 2°F (1.1°C) since the late 19th century. Most of the warming occurred in the past 40 years. The world is clearly warming, and the effects are already visible: sea level rise, extreme weather, shrinking ice sheets, ocean acidification.

title: Arctic Sea Ice Minima 2024: NASA Analysis
text: The Arctic's annual maximum sea ice extent was the 10th smallest in the satellite record, according to NASA and NSIDC. The Arctic sea ice minimum is expected to occur around September 2024, marking the lowest point of the annual cycle.

title: Antarctic Ice Sheet Losing Mass at Accelerating Rate
text: Satellite data from NASA's GRACE and GRACE-FO missions show Antarctica lost approximately 150 billion tons of ice per year between 2002 and 2023. The rate has increased by a factor of six since the early 1980s.

title: El Niño 2024: What to Expect from NASA's Forecast
text: A strong El Niño event is expected to develop in 2024, following a La Niña that lasted over three years. Historical data from NASA shows El Niño events typically cause increased rainfall in South America's western coast and drought conditions in Southeast Asia.

title: Amazon Deforestation Monitoring with NASA Satellite Data
text: Satellite data from NASA's MODIS and Landsat programs show continued deforestation in the Amazon Basin, particularly in Brazil and Peru. The Amazon rainforest loses approximately 600 km² of forest area annually, contributing to increased CO2 emissions.

title: 2023: Hottest Year on Record According to NASA/NOAA Analysis
publisher: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies
text: According to NASA GISS analysis, 2023 was the warmest year in the instrumental record, exceeding the previous record set in 2016 by 0.1°C. Global surface temperature reached +1.27°C above the 1951-1980 baseline.

title: Global Sea Level Rise: NASA Satellite Data Shows Acceleration
text: Satellite altimetry from NASA's Jason-3 and Sentinel-6 missions shows global mean sea level has risen 101.3mm since 1993, at an accelerating rate of 4.5mm/year. Thermal expansion and ice sheet melt are the primary drivers.

title: Aqua and Terra Satellites: 20+ Years of Climate Data Collection
text: NASA's Aqua and Terra satellites, launched in 2002 and 1999 respectively, continue to provide critical data on Earth's water cycle. The MODIS instrument measures land surface temperature, vegetation index (NDVI), and aerosol optical depth with unprecedented spatial resolution.

title: Global Warming Increasing Extreme Rainfall Events, NASA Study Finds
text: A comprehensive NASA study analyzing 40 years of satellite precipitation data found that extreme rainfall events have increased by approximately 15% globally since 1979. The rate of increase is faster in tropical regions and during El Niño periods.

title: Sahel Region Shows Partial Recovery from Decades of Drought
text: Despite ongoing climate challenges, the Sahel region shows signs of partial recovery from the severe droughts of the 1970s-80s. NASA POWER data indicates a modest increase in annual precipitation (about 15%) since 1984, though variability remains high.

title: Pacific Ocean Warming Affects Peruvian Anchovy Fishing Industry
text: Rising sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific Ocean, monitored by NASA's Aqua satellite (MODIS), correlate with declining anchovy catches off Peru's coast. El Niño events amplify this effect, causing warm water to push southward.

title: Greenland Ice Loss Has Accelerated 10-Fold in Two Decades, NASA Reports
text: Greenland lost an average of 279 billion tons of ice per year between 1996 and 2023, with the rate accelerating significantly since 2000. GRACE satellite data shows this contributes approximately 0.8mm/year to global sea level rise.

title: Detecting the Fingerprint of Human-Caused Climate Change, NASA Research Shows
text: Using satellite data from NASA's TRMM and GPM missions, researchers have detected a statistically significant trend in global precipitation patterns consistent with climate model predictions. The analysis covers 23 years (1998-2021) of monthly rainfall data.

title: Mountain Glaciers Worldwide Losing Mass Faster Than Projected
text: A study using NASA's GRACE and ICESat data shows that mountain glaciers worldwide lost approximately 267 gigatons of ice annually from 2000 to 2023, twice the rate calculated in earlier IPCC assessments. The Andes contributed significantly.

title: Atmospheric Water Vapor Increasing in Sync with Warming, NASA Data Shows
text: Satellite measurements from NASA's AIRS and other instruments show that atmospheric water vapor (TQV) has increased globally at a rate consistent with Clausius-Clapeyron predictions: ~7% per degree of warming. This amplifies the greenhouse effect.

title: North Atlantic Ocean Surface Temperatures Break Records in 2023
text: Sea surface temperatures in the North Atlantic reached unprecedented levels in 2023, with some regions exceeding 3°C above normal. This has implications for hurricane formation and marine ecosystems.

title: Detección de Tendencias con Mann-Kendall y Theil-Sen (Explicación Sencilla)
text: El test de Mann-Kendall evalúa si existe una tendencia monotónica (siempre subiendo o bajando) en una serie temporal. Es no paramétrico: no asume que los datos siguen una distribución normal. El estimador de Sen calcula la pendiente de la tendencia como la mediana de todas las pendientes posibles entre pares de puntos — es robusto a valores atípicos.

title: Cálculo de Anomalías y Climatología Mensual (Explicación Sencilla)
text: Una anomalía es la diferencia entre el valor observado y el promedio histórico del mismo mes (climatología). Por ejemplo, si en marzo de 2023 la temperatura fue 20°C y el promedio de todos los marzos (1981-2010) es 17°C, la anomalía de marzo 2023 es +3°C.

title: Qué Significa el Valor p en Estadística Climática
text: El valor p indica la probabilidad de obtener los resultados observados por azar si no hay tendencia real. Un valor p < 0.05 significa que es poco probable (<5%) que el patrón sea aleatorio — se considera 'estadísticamente significativo'. Pero el tamaño de la muestra y la autocorrelación afectan este cálculo.

title: Efecto de la Autocorrelación en Tendencias Climáticas (Explicación Sencilla)
text: La autocorrelación ocurre cuando valores consecutivos en una serie temporal están relacionados (ejemplo: la temperatura de enero tiende a ser similar a diciembre). Esto infla artificialmente el número de observaciones independientes y subestima el valor p. Se aplica corrección de Hamed & Rao para compensar.

title: ¿Cuántos Años Faltan para Estar Seguros? (Weatherhead et al. 1998)
text: Weatherhead et al. (1998) demostraron que para detectar una tendencia significativa, se necesitan datos de varios años — incluso si la tendencia es fuerte. Para señales pequeñas, pueden necesitarse décadas adicionales de observación. Esta 'detectabilidad' depende de la relación señal/ruido y la autocorrelación.

title: Impactos del Cambio Climático en Perú: Datos NASA
text: Perú está experimentando cambios significativos en su clima. Los glaciares tropicales de los Andes se están reduciendo rápidamente, con el 48% del hielo perdido desde 1970. Las temperaturas han aumentado 1-2°C en las últimas décadas, afectando la agricultura y el suministro de agua.

title: Retroceso de Glaciares Peruanos: Análisis NASA/NSIDC
text: Los glaciares tropicales del Perú han perdido aproximadamente 48% de su masa desde 1970, según datos de satélites NASA GRACE y mediciones in situ. La Cordillera Blanca (Huascarán) ha mostrado la mayor pérdida de hielo. Esto amenaza el suministro de agua para millones de personas en Lima y otras ciudades.

title: Inundaciones en la Costa Peruana: Análisis con Datos NASA/POWER
text: Durante el invierno de 2023, la costa peruana experimentó lluvias torrenciales atribuidas a un fenómeno El Niño moderado. Datos de NASA POWER mostraron aumentos de 400% en precipitación sobre la norma en zonas como Piura y Lambayeque, causando inundaciones severas.

title: Sequía en el Perú: Impacto en Agricultura y Recursos Hídricos
text: La sequía de 2023-2024 afectó severamente la agricultura peruana, especialmente en las regiones de Piura, Lambayeque y La Libertad. Datos del sistema GLDAS de NASA mostraron valores anómalos de humedad de suelo (GWETTOP) inferiores al percentil 10 durante varios meses consecutivos.

title: Deforestación en la Amazonía Peruana: Análisis con Datos MODIS
text: La deforestación en la Amazonía peruana alcanzó 153 km² en 2024 según análisis de MODIS y Landsat. La región de Madre de Dios es particularmente afectada por la minería ilegal de oro, que destruye ecosistemas críticos.
